Name the model. Many potential callers, each unlikely to call in a given hour, independently, at an average rate: X∼Pois(4.5) calls per hour.

(a) Pr(X=0)=e−4.5≈0.0111: about 1 hour in 90.

(b) Pr(X≥8)=1−Pr(X≤7), a sum of 8 terms, so use R:

R
dpois(0, lambda = 4.5)              # (a)
1 - ppois(7, lambda = 4.5)          # (b) Pr(X >= 8)
dpois(0, lambda = 4.5 * 20 / 60)    # (c) a 20-minute window: rate 1.5
round(dpois(0:12, 4.5), 3)          # the PMF
output
[1] 0.011109
[1] 0.08658647
[1] 0.2231302
 [1] 0.011 0.050 0.112 0.169 0.190 0.171 0.128 0.082 0.046 0.023 0.010
[12] 0.004 0.002

So Pr(X≥8)≈0.087: in roughly one afternoon hour in 11, the desk is overloaded. A manager deciding on staffing would weigh that against the cost of a third dispatcher (an expected-loss calculation again).

(c) In 20 minutes the rate is 4.5×13=1.5, so Pr(no calls)=e−1.5≈0.223.

R
d <- data.frame(x = 0:12, p = dpois(0:12, 4.5), busy = 0:12 >= 8)
ggplot(d, aes(x, p, fill = busy)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey60", "orange"), labels = c("up to 7", "8 or more")) +
  labs(x = "calls in an hour", y = "probability", fill = NULL)

Explore the Poisson distribution

Move the sliders to change the parameters and watch the shape change. The red triangle marks the expected value and the red bar spans one standard deviation either side. Move x to highlight Pr(X ≤ x); the R command that computes it is shown below. Press draw a sample to simulate 200 values: the orange lines show how often each value came up, and they sit close to the bars.

Causal Inference: Regression to the Mean: Hot Spots That Cool Down on Their Own

A police department identifies the 10 blocks with the most burglaries last year as "hot spots" and sends extra patrols. This year, burglaries on those blocks fall by 25%. Did the patrols work?

Not necessarily. Counts like burglaries vary by Poisson chance even when nothing changes. A block that had an unusually high count last year was probably partly unlucky, and next year its luck is likely to be closer to average, patrols or no patrols. Choosing units because their outcome was extreme guarantees that, on average, they'll look less extreme next time. This is regression to the mean, an effect Francis Galton called "regression towards mediocrity" in 1885–86 (the history box in Section 5.3 explains where it came from). In the simulation below, the "patrols" do nothing at all.

Hot spots that cool down on their own

A city has 100 blocks. Every block has the same true rate of burglaries, λ per year, so the counts differ only by Poisson chance. After year 1, the city labels the blocks with the highest counts as "hot spots" and sends extra patrols there. The patrols do nothing at all in this simulation. Press simulate and compare the hot spots' counts in year 1 and year 2.

The selection is the problem: last year's count caused the block to be chosen, and last year's count is related to this year's only through the block's true rate. A fair test needs a comparison group: randomly choose which hot spots get the patrols (Chapter 1), and compare treated and untreated hot spots in the same year. Real hot-spot policing studies that did exactly this did find genuine (if smaller) effects; studies that only compared before and after could not tell them apart from regression to the mean.

History: Poisson, Bortkiewicz and the Law of Small Numbers

Siméon-Denis Poisson derived the distribution in 1837, as the limit of the binomial, in a book on the probability of judgments in criminal and civil cases: he wanted to know how often juries would convict the innocent. It attracted little attention until Ladislaus Bortkiewicz showed in Das Gesetz der kleinen Zahlen (The Law of Small Numbers, 1898) how well it described rare events in large populations, from horse kicks to child suicides. Today it describes radioactive decay, network traffic, insurance claims and mutations in DNA.

Think About It: Randomness or a Cause?

A town of 20,000 people has 9 cases of a rare childhood cancer in five years, when the national rate would predict about 3. Residents suspect a chemical plant. Using Poisson reasoning, explain why this is genuinely surprising for this town, but why it might not be surprising that some town in the country has a cluster like this. What would you want to know next?

For this town, the count would be about Pois(3), and Pr(X≥9)= 1 - ppois(8, 3) ≈0.004: very unusual. But there are thousands of towns of this size, and among, say, 5,000 towns we'd expect about 5000×0.004≈20 to have such a cluster by chance alone (the birthday problem and Paul the octopus again). The cluster was noticed because it was extreme, so its surprise value is overstated. Next steps: was the cluster noticed before or after looking at many towns? Is there a plausible mechanism (exposure to a specific chemical linked to this cancer)? Do cases concentrate near the plant, and did they begin after it opened? Inference about causes needs more than an unusual count.

Key Takeaways

  • Poisson Pois(λ): counts of rare events with many independent opportunities; Pr(X=x)=e−λλx/x!.
  • It is the limit of Bin(n,λ/n) as n→∞.
  • Mean = variance = λ. Rates scale with the window: λt in a window of length t.
  • Units chosen for extreme counts tend to look less extreme next time: regression to the mean.
  • R: dpois, ppois, qpois, rpois.

4.8 Choosing the right model

The hardest part of a problem is usually not the arithmetic but deciding which distribution fits. Here are the five named distributions side by side.

Start with the mechanism: what is being counted, and how are the trials run? This flowchart asks the questions in order.

distribution the story values
Bin(n,p) successes in n independent trials, same p 0,…,n
Geom(p) failures before the 1st success 0,1,2,…
NB(r,p) failures before the rth success 0,1,2,…
hypergeometric successes in n drawn without replacement from N items with M successes 0,…,n
Pois(λ) count of rare events at average rate λ 0,1,2,…
distribution mean variance PMF in R
Bin(n,p) np np(1−p) dbinom(x, n, p)
Geom(p) 1−pp 1−pp2 dgeom(x, p)
NB(r,p) r(1−p)p r(1−p)p2 dnbinom(x, r, p)
hypergeometric nMN nMN(1−MN)N−nN−1 dhyper(x, M, N-M, n)
Pois(λ) λ λ dpois(x, lambda)

Idea: Algorithm: Which Distribution?

  1. What is being counted? Write $X = $ "the number of ...". If it isn't a count, it isn't one of these.
  2. Is there a fixed number of trials?
    • Yes, drawn with replacement or from a huge population, independent, same p: binomial.
    • Yes, drawn without replacement from a small, known population: hypergeometric.
  3. Are we waiting for something? Counting failures until the 1st success: geometric; until the rth: negative binomial.
  4. Is there only a rate, with no natural "number of trials", for events in time or space? Poisson.
  5. Check the assumptions, especially independence, and say which ones are doubtful.

Example 4.21: Which Distribution? ★ lecture example

For each situation, define X, name its distribution with parameters, and compute the probability asked for.

  1. A detective calls witnesses from a list; each, independently, has information with probability 0.2. What is the probability the first 4 calls find nothing and the 5th succeeds?
  2. A jury of 6 is chosen at random from a pool of 50 people, of whom 5 are retired police officers. What is the probability the jury includes exactly 2 of them?
  3. A forensic lab receives an average of 2.5 urgent requests per day, arriving independently. What is the probability of 5 or more on a given day?
  4. Of a company's emails, 2% are phishing attempts. In a random sample of 50 emails from its huge inbox, what is the probability there are none?

  1. We wait for the first success: X = failed calls before the first useful witness ∼Geom(0.2). "First 4 fail, 5th succeeds" is X=4: Pr(X=4)=0.84×0.2=0.0819.

  2. A fixed sample drawn without replacement from a small population: X = officers on the jury, hypergeometric with N=50, M=5, n=6. Pr(X=2)=(52)(454)(506)≈0.0938. (The sample is 12% of the population, so the binomial would not be a safe approximation here.)

  3. Events at a rate, with no fixed number of trials: X∼Pois(2.5). Pr(X≥5)=1−Pr(X≤4)≈0.109.

  4. A fixed number of emails from a huge population, independent, same p: X∼Bin(50,0.02). Pr(X=0)=0.9850≈0.364. (A Poisson with λ=50×0.02=1 gives e−1=0.368: close, as the limit theorem promises.)

R
dgeom(4, 0.2)                                  # 1
dhyper(2, m = 5, n = 45, k = 6)                # 2
1 - ppois(4, 2.5)                              # 3
dbinom(0, 50, 0.02); dpois(0, 1)               # 4, and its Poisson approximation
output
[1] 0.08192
[1] 0.09376239
[1] 0.108822
[1] 0.3641697
[1] 0.3678794

Check Yourself

Is there a fixed number of yes/no trials, or a count of events at an average rate?

A count of rare events at a rate: Poisson, with λ=500×0.3=150 for the whole transcript.

Poisson

Is the sampling with or without replacement? Is the sample a small fraction of the population?

Without replacement, and 10 is a quarter of the 40 pills: hypergeometric with N=40, M=6, n=10.

hypergeometric

Is the number of calls fixed in advance, or does it keep going until something happens? How many successes are needed?

Waiting for the 3rd success: negative binomial with r=3, p=0.01; the expected number of failed calls is 3×0.99/0.01=297.

negative binomial

Strictly, sampling is without replacement. But how big is the sample compared with the population?

A fixed number of independent-enough trials with the same p: binomial, Bin(1000,0.02). Strictly hypergeometric, but the sample is a tiny fraction of millions, so the binomial is essentially exact. (A Poisson with λ=20 would also be a fine approximation.)

binomial

Key Takeaways

  • Start by writing $X = $ "the number of ...".
  • Fixed trials with replacement: binomial; without replacement from a small population: hypergeometric; waiting: geometric or negative binomial; a rate: Poisson.
  • Every model rests on assumptions, usually independence. Name them, and ask what happens if they fail.

Prediction and inference in this chapter

Every distribution in this chapter is a model of a mechanism with a few parameters, and every example used it in one of two directions.

  • Prediction (parameters known, outcome unknown): the expected cost of overbooking, the chance a guesser passes a quiz, the number of boxes needed to collect six toys, the number of calls a dispatch desk must handle. Expected values give the best guess under squared loss; standard deviations and quantiles say how far off it may be; and the best decision (how many tickets, how many dispatchers) minimizes an expected loss.
  • Inference (outcome observed, mechanism uncertain): was Paul the octopus guessing? Could Muriel Bristol really taste the difference? Were the V-1 bombs aimed? How big is a hidden population? In each case we asked how probable the observed data would be under a simple "nothing special is going on" mechanism, and found it either plausible (the bombs, the horse kicks) or surprising (all four cups right). The capture–recapture example went one step further and chose the parameter value that made the data most probable: maximum likelihood.

Chapters 8 and 9 turn these informal arguments into estimates with margins of error and into formal tests. They will need one more ingredient first: how averages of random variables behave, which is the subject of Chapters 6 and 7.

4.9 Interludes

Interlude (Optional): Moment Generating Functions

The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is MX(t)=E[etX]=∑xetxp(x), for the values of t where the sum is finite. It looks like an odd thing to compute, but it packs all the moments E[X],E[X2],… into one function. Expanding etX=1+tX+t2X22!+⋯ and taking expectations term by term gives MX(t)=1+tE[X]+t22!E[X2]+⋯, so differentiating and setting t=0 picks out the moments: MX′(0)=E[X] and MX″(0)=E[X2].

Three examples.

  • Bernoulli: M(t)=(1−p)e0+pet=1−p+pet.
  • Binomial: X is a sum of n independent Bernoullis, and for independent random variables E[et(X+Y)]=E[etX]E[etY] (Chapter 6), so M(t)=(1−p+pet)n. Differentiating, M′(0)=n(1−p+p)n−1p=np.
  • Poisson: M(t)=∑xetxe−λλxx!=e−λ∑x(λet)xx!=e−λeλet=eλ(et−1).

Two powerful facts. First, an MGF (when it exists near t=0) determines the distribution uniquely. Second, the MGF of a sum of independent random variables is the product of their MGFs. Together they give slick proofs. For example, if X∼Pois(λ) and Y∼Pois(μ) are independent, then MX+Y(t)=eλ(et−1)eμ(et−1)=e(λ+μ)(et−1), which is the MGF of Pois(λ+μ). So independent Poisson counts add up to a Poisson count: calls to two separate desks, at rates 4.5 and 3 per hour, total Pois(7.5).

Why it matters: MGFs are the main tool for proving the Central Limit Theorem in Chapter 7.

Interlude (Optional): Entropy: How Surprising Is a Random Variable?

Section 2.6 met Shannon's entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a categorical variable is. It applies to any discrete random variable: H(X)=−∑xp(x)log2p(x)bits. The quantity −log2p(x) is the surprise of seeing the value x: a sure thing (p=1) carries 0 bits of surprise, a fair coin flip 1 bit, and a one-in-a-million event about 20 bits. Entropy is the expected surprise, E[−log2p(X)], computed with the expectation rule of Section 4.2.

For a Bernoulli trial, H=−plog2p−(1−p)log2(1−p):

R
p <- seq(0.001, 0.999, by = 0.001)
H <- -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)
ggplot(data.frame(p, H), aes(p, H)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "success probability p", y = "entropy H (bits)")

It is largest, 1 bit, at p=12, and zero when the outcome is certain, just like the variance p(1−p), though entropy and variance are not the same thing: entropy doesn't care what the values are, only how probable they are.

Shannon proved that H(X) is the smallest possible average number of bits needed to record outcomes of X, which is the foundation of every compression format from ZIP to MP3. And a password chosen uniformly from mk possibilities has entropy klog2m bits: about 52 bits for 8 characters from 94 symbols (Example 3.7). Security experts measure password strength in exactly these bits, and a password people actually choose has far fewer.

Why it matters: entropy turns "how uncertain?" into a number, and underlies information theory, compression, cryptography and the cross-entropy loss used to train classifiers.

Bayesian Inference: Learning a Success Probability

In Example 4.10 we knew the false-positive rate p. Usually we don't, and must learn it from data. The Bayesian approach treats the unknown p like the suspects in Chapter 3's detective story. Suppose p could be any of 0,0.1,0.2,…,1, all equally plausible at first (the prior). We then see 7 successes in 10 independent trials. For each candidate value of p, the likelihood of the data is the binomial probability (107)p7(1−p)3. Multiply prior by likelihood and rescale:

R
p_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)
prior <- rep(1 / 11, 11)
likelihood <- dbinom(7, size = 10, prob = p_grid)
posterior <- prior * likelihood / sum(prior * likelihood)
round(posterior, 3)
d <- rbind(data.frame(p = p_grid, prob = prior, which = "prior"),
           data.frame(p = p_grid, prob = posterior, which = "posterior, 7 of 10"))
d$which <- factor(d$which, levels = c("prior", "posterior, 7 of 10"))
ggplot(d, aes(p, prob)) + geom_col(width = 0.06) + facet_wrap(~ which) +
  labs(x = "candidate value of p", y = "probability")
output
 [1] 0.000 0.000 0.001 0.010 0.047 0.129 0.236 0.293 0.221 0.063 0.000

The posterior piles up around 0.7, the observed fraction, but still gives real weight to 0.6 and 0.8: ten trials can't pin p down exactly. More data would narrow it further. Chapter 5 replaces the grid of 11 candidates with every value between 0 and 1, which leads to the beta distribution.

4.10 Exercises

Each exercise has a hint and an answer. Start every word problem by writing $X = $ "the number of ..." and naming its distribution.

Exercises

  1. A PMF by hand. Roll two fair dice and let M be the larger of the two numbers. (a) Find the PMF of M by counting outcomes. (b) Find E[M]. (c) Find Pr(M≤3) using the CDF.

    Use the 6 × 6 grid (the random-variable widget in Section 3.8 has a "larger of the two dice" option). How many of the 36 outcomes have a maximum of exactly 1? Of exactly 2? Look for the pattern 2m−1.

    (a) Pr(M=m)=2m−136 for m=1,…,6: that is 136,336,536,736,936,1136. (b) E[M]=1+6+15+28+45+6636=16136≈4.47. (c) F(3)=1+3+536=936=0.25; equivalently both dice are at most 3, (36)2.

  2. Expected value and variance. A random variable takes the values −1, 0 and 2 with probabilities 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2. Find E[X], Var[X], E[5−2X] and SD[5−2X].

    Compute E[X] and E[X2] first, then use the shortcut formula and the rules for aX+b.

    E[X]=−0.3+0+0.4=0.1; E[X2]=0.3+0+0.8=1.1; Var[X]=1.1−0.01=1.09. E[5−2X]=5−0.2=4.8; SD[5−2X]=21.09≈2.09.

  3. Insurance. A phone insurance policy costs $120 a year. In a year, 4% of phones are lost or stolen (the insurer pays $900) and another 10% are damaged (the insurer pays $250). (a) Find the insurer's expected profit per policy. (b) Find the standard deviation of its profit. (c) Explain why the insurer cares about the expected value but a customer might not.

    The insurer's profit takes three values: 120, 120−900 and 120−250. Write its PMF, then compute E and SD as in Examples 4.5 and 4.8.

    Profit 120 (prob 0.86), −780 (0.04), −130 (0.10). (a) E=103.2−31.2−13=$59. (b) E[profit2]=0.86×14400+0.04×608400+0.10×16900=12384+24336+1690=38410, so Var=38410−592=34929 and SD≈$187. (c) The insurer sells thousands of policies, so by the Law of Large Numbers its average profit per policy will be very close to $59. A customer buys one policy and faces one outcome; they pay $59 on average to avoid a possible $900 loss they might not be able to afford.

  4. Binomial. A fingerprint examiner makes an error on 3% of comparisons, independently. In a week she makes 40 comparisons. (a) What is the probability of no errors? (b) Of at least 2 errors? (c) What are the mean and standard deviation of the number of errors? (d) Is independence plausible here? Explain.

    X∼Bin(40,0.03). For (b), Pr(X≥2)=1−Pr(X≤1), which is 1 - pbinom(1, 40, 0.03) in R.

    (a) 0.9740≈0.296. (b) 1−0.296−40(0.03)(0.9739)≈1−0.296−0.366=0.338. (c) Mean 1.2, SD 40×0.03×0.97≈1.08. (d) Doubtful: errors may cluster, for example on difficult partial prints, at the end of a long day, or on cases with misleading context information, so one error makes others more likely.

  5. Geometric. A password-guessing program tries passwords from a list of common passwords in random order, and each guess independently has a 1-in-50 chance of being right for a given account. (a) What is the expected number of wrong guesses before success? (b) What is the probability it needs more than 100 guesses in total? (c) The program has already made 100 wrong guesses. What is the probability it needs more than another 100?

    X∼Geom(0.02) counts wrong guesses. "More than 100 guesses in total" means the first 100 are all wrong. For (c), use memorylessness.

    (a) 0.98/0.02=49 wrong guesses (50 guesses in all, on average). (b) Pr(X≥100)=0.98100≈0.133. (c) By memorylessness, also 0.98100≈0.133: the 100 failures so far don't make success any closer. (In reality, guessing without repeating passwords from a finite list isn't memoryless, but the model says each guess is a fresh independent chance.)

  6. Hypergeometric. An evidence locker holds 30 bags, of which 8 have been tampered with. An auditor inspects 5 bags chosen at random. (a) What is the probability she finds no tampered bags? (b) At least one? (c) Compare (a) with the binomial approximation and explain the difference.

    N=30, M=8, n=5. In R: dhyper(0, m = 8, n = 22, k = 5). The binomial would use p=8/30.

    (a) (225)/(305)=26334/142506≈0.185. (b) 1−0.185=0.815. (c) The binomial gives (22/30)5≈0.212, noticeably higher. The sample is 1/6 of the population, and each untampered bag drawn makes the next draw more likely to be tampered, so missing every tampered bag is less likely than the binomial suggests.

  7. Poisson. A website receives login attacks at an average rate of 3 per minute, independently. (a) What is the probability of no attacks in a given minute? (b) Of more than 6 in a minute? (c) Of at least 10 in a 2-minute window?

    One minute: Pois(3). Two minutes: Pois(6). "More than 6" is 1−Pr(X≤6).

    (a) e−3≈0.050. (b) 1 - ppois(6, 3) ≈0.034. (c) 1 - ppois(9, 6) ≈0.084.

  8. Poisson approximation. A rare blood type occurs in 0.4% of people. A blood drive collects 500 donations. Find the probability of at least 3 donations with the rare type (a) exactly, with the binomial, and (b) with the Poisson approximation. Why is the approximation good here?

    Binomial: Bin(500,0.004). Poisson: λ=np.

    (a) 1 - pbinom(2, 500, 0.004) ≈0.323. (b) λ=2; 1 - ppois(2, 2) ≈0.323. The approximation is excellent because n is large and p is small: many chances, each rare, exactly the setting of the Poisson limit theorem.

  9. Is it Poisson? R's InsectSprays counts insects on plots. For spray C, the 12 counts are 0, 1, 7, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1, 4. (a) Compute the sample mean and variance. (b) Is a Poisson model plausible? (c) Using a Poisson with λ equal to the sample mean, how many of the 12 plots would you expect to have 0 insects? Compare with the data.

    x <- InsectSprays$count[InsectSprays$spray == "C"], then mean(x) and var(x). For (c), compute 12 * dpois(0, mean(x)).

    (a) Mean 25/12≈2.08, variance ≈3.90. (b) The variance is nearly twice the mean, so the counts are more variable than a Poisson (called overdispersion), largely because of the plot with 7 insects; with only 12 counts, though, the evidence is weak. (c) 12e−2.08≈1.5 plots expected, and 2 were observed: reasonably close.

  10. Linearity with indicators. At a party, 30 guests check their coats, and the coats are returned at random. (a) What is the expected number of guests who get their own coat back? (b) A city has 200 intersections, and each has a camera that works on a given day with probability 0.97, not necessarily independently. What is the expected number of working cameras, and why don't you need independence?

    Write each count as a sum of indicators, as in Example 4.7. Linearity of expectation doesn't require independence.

    (a) Each guest gets their own coat with probability 130, so the expected number is 30×130=1. (b) 200×0.97=194. E[I1+⋯+I200]=E[I1]+⋯+E[I200] holds whatever the dependence; independence would matter for the variance (for example, a citywide power cut would knock out many cameras at once).

  11. Which model? For each, define X, name the distribution and its parameters, and state one assumption that might fail. (a) The number of jurors, out of 12, who have served on a jury before, if 30% of the jury pool has. (b) The number of murders in a city next month, which averages 25 per month. (c) The number of houses a burglar tries before finding an unlocked one, if 10% of houses are unlocked. (d) The number of women on a 5-person panel chosen at random from 9 men and 6 women.

    Use the algorithm in Section 4.8: fixed trials or waiting? With or without replacement from a small group? Or just a rate?

    (a) Bin(12,0.3); jurors aren't independent draws if the pool is small (then hypergeometric). (b) Pois(25); murders can cluster (a single incident with several victims, retaliation), breaking independence. (c) Geom(0.1); a burglar doesn't choose houses at random, and unlocked houses may cluster on certain streets. (d) Hypergeometric with N=15, M=6, n=5; assumes the panel really is chosen at random.

  12. Regression to the mean. A school district names its 5 lowest-scoring schools (out of 100) as "failing" and gives them extra tutoring. Next year, their average score rises noticeably. (a) Give a reason this could happen even if the tutoring had no effect. (b) Design a better way to evaluate the tutoring.

    Test scores vary by chance from year to year. Why were these 5 schools chosen? Think about the hot-spots widget in Section 4.7.

    (a) The schools were chosen because their scores were unusually low. Part of a low score is bad luck (a difficult year, a few absent students), and next year's luck is likely to be closer to average, so their scores would tend to rise anyway: regression to the mean. (b) Among the low-scoring schools, randomly choose which ones get tutoring and compare the change in scores between tutored and untutored schools over the same year.

  13. How long should a quiz be? A teacher wants a true/false quiz on which a student who guesses every answer has less than a 5% chance of scoring 70% or more. Using quizzes of 10, 20 or 30 questions, which is the shortest that works?

    A guesser's score is Bin(n,0.5). "70% or more" of 10 questions is at least 7 right, so compute Pr(X≥7)=1−Pr(X≤6) = 1 - pbinom(6, 10, 0.5), and similarly for 20 (at least 14) and 30 (at least 21).

    10 questions: Pr(X≥7)≈0.172. 20 questions: Pr(X≥14)≈0.058, just too high. 30 questions: Pr(X≥21)≈0.021. So 30 questions. More questions make it harder to do well by luck, because the guesser's fraction correct concentrates around 0.5 (the Law of Large Numbers again).

  14. Are great discoveries Poisson? Using R's discoveries (Example 4.2), (a) compare the mean and variance of the yearly counts. (b) Compute the number of years out of 100 that a Poisson distribution with the same mean predicts for 0 to 6 discoveries, and compare with the data. (c) Suggest a reason for any mismatch.

    d <- as.numeric(discoveries); then mean(d), var(d) and round(100 * dpois(0:6, mean(d)), 1). Compare with table(d). Remember the Poisson's fingerprint.

    (a) Mean 3.1, variance 5.08: much bigger than the mean, so the counts are overdispersed. (b) Poisson predicts about 4.5, 14.0, 21.6, 22.4, 17.3, 10.7 and 5.6 years with 0 to 6 discoveries, against 9, 12, 26, 20, 12, 7 and 6 observed; it predicts too few years with 0 and with 7 or more (3.9 predicted, 8 observed). (c) The Poisson assumes a constant rate, but discoveries came in bursts (eras of rapid progress, and quieter periods such as wartime), so the rate itself varied from year to year. A varying rate makes counts more spread out than a single Poisson. The negative binomial is often used for such overdispersed counts.

  15. Settling in Catan. In the board game Settlers of Catan, two dice are rolled every turn, and a settlement collects one resource whenever the total matches the number on an adjacent tile. (a) A settlement touches tiles numbered 6, 8 and 9. What is the expected number of resources it collects per roll? (b) Over 60 rolls? (c) Compare a settlement on tiles 2, 3 and 12. Why do experienced players avoid it?

    Write the number collected per roll as a sum of three indicators, one per tile. Pr(total=6)=536; use the dice-total distribution from Example 3.22 for the others, then linearity.

    (a) 536+536+436=1436≈0.39 resources per roll. (b) 60×1436≈23.3. (c) 1+2+136=436≈0.11 per roll, about 6.7 in 60 rolls: less than a third as productive. (The game prints the "hot" numbers 6 and 8 in red for this reason.)
